newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts confused by Riksbank policy statement.
newsitem.headline: Analysts confused by Riksbank policy statement.

text.p: Statements by the Swedish central bank, the Riksbank, earlier this week that monetary policy would not necessarily follow the same pattern as in the past has created confusion on the market, analysts said on Friday.

Whilst some players interpret the comments to mean that it will up the size of cuts to its key interest rates, others say the cuts will be smaller and a third group believe the Riksbank is referring to the interval between rate reductions.

"We think the Riksbank will increase the pace of its cuts, and we have lowered the forecast for where the repo rate will bottom out to four percent from 4.5 percent," Handelsbanken economist Marie Giertz told Reuters.
The repo rate, which is the central bank's main monetary tool, was cut to 4.95 percent from 5.05 percent on Tuesday.
The reason for Handelsbanken's forecast revision is that the Riksbank's emphasis that inflation prospects are looking better than expected, she said.
"Our interpretation is that the Riksbank has cut too little and that it is now trying to remedy this," Giertz added.

Handelsbanken believes that the Riksbank will cut the repo rate by 10 basis points on Tuesday and follow up with a 50 basis point reduction in its deposit and lending rate corridor at the next board meeting on October 24.
This would be followed up by a sequence of 20 basis point cuts every other week, Giertz said.
Many players had expected the Riksbank to lower its deposit and lending rates, currently set at 4.75 percent and 6.25 percent respectively, after its last meeting on Thursday.
Tomas Niemela of Aragon stockbrokers said a change in the pattern could simply mean divergence from the existing two-week rate cut interval.

"I think the Riksbank will break the weekly pattern so that they don't have to show what's on the agenda all the time," he said, adding that this would bring them into line with the way foreign central banks tend to act.
Niemela's interpretation is supported by comments by deputy Riksbank governor Lars Heikensten that he hoped to move the monetary policy debate towards larger, more important issues.

Bjorn Englund of Unibank Markets said that although it was possible that the Riksbank wanted to break the two-week pattern, the question would be why it would want to change something that worked well.
"It's a good thing that they signal that the bottom is further off, but let's keep it to 10 basis point cuts every other week so as to minimise speculation," he said.
Englund believes that Heikensten's comments were unnecessary and served only to create confusion.
Heikensten's comments at a financial seminar on Wednesday were as follows:

"Our judgement made in mid-September -- which is still valid -- was that available information suggested there was still some room to cut the repo rate. On the other hand, you can't always expect monetary policy to follow a certain pattern in the future."
